questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with urge incontinence has a new prescription for oxybutynin (Ditropan). Before giving the first dose, which findings should the nurse report to the health care provider? Select all that apply.
options: History of glaucoma
Urinary frequency of 12 times a day
Post-void residual of 500 mL on bladder scan
Reports waking twice a night to void
Reports episodes of leaking when unable to reach the toilet in time after a strong urge
optionRationales: Correct. Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic, which should be avoided in clients with glaucoma.
Frequency is one of the problems this drug is meant to reduce. It is the reason for the prescription, not a reason to hold it.
Correct. Anticholinergics reduce bladder contractions. A bladder that is already retaining 500 mL after voiding could retain even more, so the provider needs to know.
Nighttime voiding is part of the urge incontinence picture the medication is treating.
Leaking after a strong urge is the urge incontinence the drug is prescribed to treat.
questions.rationale: Anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin reduce urinary frequency and treat incontinence by calming bladder contractions. The slides note significant side effects and say to avoid them in glaucoma. A large post-void residual means the bladder is already not emptying, and a drug that relaxes the bladder could make retention worse. Symptoms of urge incontinence are the reason to give it.
questions.takeaway: Oxybutynin (anticholinergic): reduces frequency and incontinence. Avoid in glaucoma, and watch for retention.
questions.hintContent: Recall what anticholinergic medications do to the bladder and the contraindication highlighted on the slides.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate findings that are the reason for the drug (its indication) from findings that make the drug unsafe.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A postoperative client with urinary retention is started on bethanechol (Urecholine). Which finding best indicates the medication is having the intended effect?
options: The client voids 350 mL, and a bladder scan afterward shows 40 mL
The client reports making fewer trips to the bathroom each day and night
The client's urine has turned a reddish-orange color
The client reports less burning with urination
optionRationales: Correct. Bethanechol is a cholinergic drug that promotes urination. Voiding a good volume with little left behind shows the bladder is emptying.
Fewer voids is the goal of anticholinergic drugs used for frequency, the opposite of bethanechol's action.
Reddish-orange urine is the expected effect of phenazopyridine (Pyridium), not bethanechol.
Less burning would reflect a urinary analgesic, which treats pain rather than retention.
questions.rationale: Cholinergic medications such as bethanechol stimulate the bladder to contract and promote urination, so effectiveness shows up as better emptying: a good voided volume and a small post-void residual. The nurse also monitors for elevated liver and pancreatic enzyme levels. Fewer voids, discolored urine, and pain relief are the effects of other drug classes.
questions.takeaway: Bethanechol (cholinergic) promotes urination. Success is good voiding with a low residual.
questions.hintContent: Contrast cholinergic and anticholinergic effects on the bladder, and link each urinary drug class to its expected effect.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the drug's purpose (it treats retention), then choose the finding that shows that problem is resolving.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with painful urination from a urinary tract infection is prescribed an antibiotic and phenazopyridine (Pyridium). Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?
options: "Once the burning stops, I can stop taking my antibiotic."
"If my urine changes color, I should stop taking this medicine and call the clinic right away."
"My urine may turn reddish-orange, and this drug may make me a little drowsy."
"This medicine will make me void more often to flush out the infection."
optionRationales: Phenazopyridine only relieves pain. It does not treat the infection, so the antibiotic must be finished.
A color change is an expected effect, not a reason to stop.
Correct. Phenazopyridine discolors urine (reddish-orange) and can be slightly sedating, so this statement shows understanding.
Increasing urine output is the action of a diuretic. Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic.
questions.rationale: Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic: it treats the pain of dysuria but not the infection itself, which is the antibiotic's job. Its expected effects are discolored urine and mild sedation. Clients need to know the color change is harmless and that they must finish the antibiotic even after the pain eases.
questions.takeaway: Pyridium relieves pain only. Urine turns reddish-orange and it can be mildly sedating. Finish the antibiotic.
questions.hintContent: Recall the drug class of phenazopyridine, its two side effects on the slides, and the role of the antibiotic.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement against what the drug does and does not do. A correct statement matches both its purpose and its expected effects.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for three clients: one taking furosemide (Lasix), one taking hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), and one taking spironolactone (Aldactone). Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Spironolactone: avoid salt substitutes
Furosemide: your blood will be checked for kidney function (BUN and creatinine), potassium, and sodium
Spironolactone: use a potassium-based salt substitute to replace the potassium you lose
HCTZ: expect blood tests to monitor BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium
Furosemide: this medicine does not affect your blood levels, so no lab work is needed
Hydrochlorothiazide: take a potassium-based salt substitute at each meal
optionRationales: Correct. Spironolactone is potassium-sparing, and most salt substitutes contain potassium, so the combination can raise potassium too high.
Correct. Loop diuretics such as furosemide require monitoring of BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium.
Spironolactone keeps potassium in the body. Adding potassium from a salt substitute is the danger the slides warn against.
Correct. Thiazide diuretics such as HCTZ require the same monitoring of BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium.
Furosemide changes fluid and electrolyte balance, which is why labs are monitored.
Potassium replacement for a diuretic is ordered by the provider based on lab results. Clients should not start using a salt substitute on their own.
questions.rationale: All three diuretic types change fluid and electrolyte balance, so BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium are monitored for each. The key difference is that spironolactone is potassium-sparing. Clients taking it must avoid salt substitutes, which are potassium-based. Clients should not change their potassium intake on their own. Lab results guide any change.
questions.takeaway: Lasix, HCTZ, Aldactone: monitor BUN, creatinine, K⁺, and Na⁺. Aldactone spares K⁺, so no salt substitutes.
questions.hintContent: Recall the monitoring the slides list for each diuretic and which diuretic keeps potassium in the body.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each statement for the drug named. Watch for options that pair a potassium source with a potassium-sparing drug.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client taking spironolactone (Aldactone) for hypertension says, "I've cut out regular salt and switched to a salt substitute instead." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "That's a healthy change. Salt substitutes are a great choice while you take your blood pressure medication."
"Please stop the salt substitute. Most contain potassium, which this drug holds in your body."
"Take your spironolactone at night so it won't interact with the salt substitute."
"You can go back to using regular table salt, since your medicine removes the extra sodium."
optionRationales: Praising the switch misses the danger: salt substitutes are potassium-based, and spironolactone spares potassium.

Correct. Spironolactone is potassium-sparing. Adding potassium from a salt substitute risks too much potassium, so the client should stop it. The nurse then lets the provider know so labs can be checked.
The timing of the dose does not prevent potassium from building up.
Returning to table salt works against blood pressure control and does not address the real issue.
questions.rationale: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic, and the slides specifically say to avoid salt substitutes, which are made with potassium. The safe response stops the extra potassium source. The nurse then informs the provider, who monitors BUN, creatinine, potassium, and sodium. Cutting sodium is good, but not by adding potassium.
questions.takeaway: Potassium-sparing diuretic plus a potassium salt substitute risks too much potassium. Tell the client to stop the substitute.
questions.hintContent: Connect what spironolactone does to potassium with what most salt substitutes contain.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the hidden risk in the client's statement, then choose the response that removes the risk and involves the provider.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.stem: A client with anuria and a GFR of 10 mL/min is starting peritoneal dialysis. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the treatment?
options: "My blood will be pumped through a machine outside my body and then returned."
"Once my kidneys recover, I will only need treatments about once a month."
"This treatment is used when the kidneys work normally but the bladder will not empty."
"Fluid will be put into my abdomen and then drained, and I'll need to do this often."
optionRationales: Circulating blood through an external machine describes hemodialysis.
Peritoneal dialysis must be done at frequent intervals, and a client with a GFR of 10 mL/min has severely reduced kidney function.
Dialysis is for severely reduced or absent kidney function, not for a bladder that cannot empty.
Correct. In peritoneal dialysis, dialysis solution is instilled into the abdominal cavity and drained, and it must be done at frequent intervals.
questions.rationale: Dialysis replaces kidney function when it is severely reduced or absent. Anuria (<100 mL/day) and a GFR of 10 mL/min (normal is 90–110) show this client's kidneys are barely filtering. Hemodialysis sends blood through an external machine. Peritoneal dialysis instills solution into the abdominal cavity and must be repeated frequently.
questions.takeaway: Hemodialysis: blood goes through an external machine. Peritoneal dialysis: solution goes into the abdomen, done frequently.
questions.hintContent: Link the client's anuria and low GFR to why dialysis is needed, then distinguish the two types of dialysis.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which option describes the type of dialysis in the stem and which options describe hemodialysis or a different problem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: An older adult with urinary incontinence is being discharged home with an indwelling urinary catheter and will be cared for by a daughter. Which actions should the nurse include in discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: Refer to a home health nurse for follow-up catheter care
Arrange delivery of catheter supplies through a medical supply company
Wait to teach the daughter until a problem occurs at home
Refer to an occupational therapist for help with adapting toileting and self-care
Include the daughter in catheter care teaching before discharge
Refer to a respiratory therapist for catheter teaching
optionRationales: Correct. A home health nurse is one of the referrals the slides list for continuing care after discharge.
Correct. A medical supply company provides the catheter supplies the client will need at home.
Teaching should happen before discharge, so the caregiver is prepared and problems are prevented.
Correct. An occupational therapist can help the client adapt daily activities, including toileting.
Correct. Family members and caregivers should be included in collaborative care.
A respiratory therapist is not the right discipline for urinary catheter teaching.
questions.rationale: Collaborative care for urinary problems often includes referrals before or after discharge: a wound and ostomy nurse, an occupational therapist, a home health nurse, and a medical supply company. Family members and caregivers are included. This collaboration matters most when the client goes home or to long-term care. Teaching is done ahead of time, not after a problem happens.
questions.takeaway: Discharge for urinary problems: home health, OT, wound and ostomy nurse, medical supplies, and teach the caregiver early.
questions.hintContent: Recall the collaborative referrals listed on the slides and when caregivers should be taught.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the actions that send the right discipline and prepare the caregiver before discharge.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse observes an assistive personnel (AP) caring for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene immediately?
options: Cleans the perineum and catheter with soap and water, moving away from the meatus
Lays the drainage bag on the client's abdomen during a transfer to a stretcher
Secures the catheter tubing to the client's thigh
Empties the bag into a graduated container labeled for this client
optionRationales: Cleaning from the meatus outward moves organisms away from the urethra, which is correct technique.
Correct. Raising the bag above the bladder lets urine flow back into the bladder, which raises the risk of a urinary tract infection. This needs to be corrected right away.
Securing the tubing prevents pulling on the catheter and urethral injury.
Using a separate labeled container for each client prevents cross-contamination and allows accurate output measurement.
questions.rationale: Catheter care relies on aseptic technique. The drainage bag must stay below the level of the bladder so urine always flows away from it. Holding the bag above the bladder allows backflow of urine that may carry bacteria. The other actions are correct parts of catheter care and accurate I&O.
questions.takeaway: Keep the drainage bag below the bladder at all times to prevent backflow and infection.
questions.hintContent: Connect catheter care principles (aseptic technique, gravity drainage) to infection risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the action that breaks a safety principle and could cause harm right now.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Interventions, Medications & Dialysis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with a urinary tract infection has dysuria and frequency and has no fluid restrictions. Which independent nursing intervention is the priority to include in the plan of care?
options: Encourage at least 2,000 mL of fluid daily, spaced through the day
Restrict fluids to reduce the number of painful voids
Ask the provider for a cholinergic medication to help promote voiding
Insert an indwelling catheter to measure output accurately
optionRationales: Correct. Increasing fluid intake is an independent intervention that dilutes urine and flushes the urinary tract. Spreading it out avoids overloading the bladder at once.
Limiting fluids concentrates the urine, which irritates the bladder wall more, and reduces flushing of the urinary tract.
Requesting a medication is collaborative, not independent, and a cholinergic is for retention, not infection.
An indwelling catheter needs an order and increases infection risk. It is not indicated here.
questions.rationale: Increased fluid intake is one of the main independent interventions for urinary problems when not contraindicated. Dilute urine is less irritating to the bladder, and frequent voiding helps flush bacteria out. Restricting fluids is a common misconception because it seems to reduce painful voids, but it concentrates the urine. Catheters and medications require orders and are not the best choice here.
questions.takeaway: Unless fluid is restricted, encourage about 2 L or more a day, spaced out, for urinary health.
questions.hintContent: Recall which urinary interventions are independent and how fluid intake affects urine concentration and bladder irritation.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that need a provider's order, then choose the independent action that treats the cause.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: A term newborn is 40 hours old and has not voided since birth. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the finding, since healthy newborns often do not void until 72 hours of age
Notify the provider immediately and prepare for catheterization
Give the newborn supplemental water to stimulate voiding
Assess feeding intake and check for bladder distention, restlessness, and pain
optionRationales: Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours, so 40 hours without voiding is not normal.
The provider will need to know, but the nurse first gathers assessment data to report. Catheterization is not the first step.
Giving water is not an appropriate independent action for a newborn and skips assessment.

Correct. The slides direct the nurse to assess fluid intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain. This newborn is past 24 hours and nearing the 48-hour mark, so the nurse gathers these data quickly to report.
questions.rationale: Healthy newborns void within the first 24 hours, and it is important to make sure they void within 48 hours of delivery. At 40 hours, the nurse must act, starting with a focused assessment of intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain. These findings shape the report to the provider. Ignoring the finding or jumping to an invasive step skips the assessment.
questions.takeaway: Newborns should void within 24 hours, and must by 48 hours. Assess intake, bladder distention, restlessness, and pain.
questions.hintContent: Recall the newborn voiding time frames and the assessments the slides recommend.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether this finding is normal. Then choose the action that gathers the data the provider will need.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The nurse in a pediatric clinic reviews parent reports. Which findings are expected for the child's age? Select all that apply.
options: Newborn: urine looks slightly cloudy in the diaper
3-year-old: stays dry during the day but still wets at night
9-year-old: voids about seven times a day
10-year-old: has new daytime wetting episodes at school
5-year-old: wets the bed most nights and is a very deep sleeper
2-month-old: urine is consistently dark amber
optionRationales: Correct. Newborn urine may be cloudy.
Correct. Most children develop urinary control between 2 and 5 years, and daytime control normally comes before nighttime control.
Correct. School-age children urinate six to eight times a day.
Daytime (diurnal) enuresis in a school-age child may be pathologic and needs follow-up.
Correct. Nighttime bedwetting is common in deep sleepers and is not considered a problem until after 7 years of age.
Urine in early infancy should be straw-colored. Persistently dark urine suggests the infant may not be getting enough fluid.
questions.rationale: Normal urinary patterns change with age. Newborn urine may be cloudy, and in early infancy it is straw-colored. Toddlers and preschoolers gain daytime control before nighttime control. School-age children void six to eight times a day, and nocturnal enuresis is not a problem until after age 7. Diurnal enuresis in a school-age child, or dark urine in an infant, needs follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Day control before night control. Bedwetting is OK until age 7, but daytime wetting in school-age children may be pathologic.
questions.hintContent: Recall the urinary milestones and normal findings from newborn through school age.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each finding against the child's age. The same behavior can be normal at one age and a concern at another.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: A client at 34 weeks of pregnancy says, "I'm going to the bathroom all the time again. It got better for a few months. Is something wrong?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Cut back to about 1 liter of fluid a day so you won't have to void as often."
"Frequency should have gone away after the first trimester, so I'll let your provider know about it."
"The growing uterus presses on the bladder again late in pregnancy. Report any burning or fever."
"Frequency usually means gestational diabetes, so you will need a glucose test."
optionRationales: Restricting fluids can lead to dehydration and concentrated urine and is not recommended.
Frequency usually decreases in the second trimester and returns in the third, so this is not abnormal.

Correct. Pressure from the enlarging uterus causes frequency, which eases in the second trimester and returns in the third. Pregnant clients are at risk for UTI, so reporting burning or fever is appropriate.
Frequency from uterine pressure is expected and does not point to gestational diabetes.
questions.rationale: The enlarging uterus presses against the bladder and increases urinary frequency. The symptom decreases during the second trimester and comes back in the third. The nurse reassures the client while teaching her to report signs of infection, since UTI is a risk in pregnancy. Fluid restriction is never the answer to normal frequency.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy frequency: present early, eases in the 2nd trimester, returns in the 3rd. Teach UTI warning signs.
questions.hintContent: Recall how urinary frequency changes across the trimesters and why.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether the symptom is expected at 34 weeks. Then choose the response that reassures accurately and keeps the client safe.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: A client in her second trimester has glucose in a routine urinalysis. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: It confirms gestational diabetes and requires insulin therapy
It is always a normal finding during pregnancy and needs no further follow-up or evaluation
Increased filtration can cause it, but it needs follow-up to rule out gestational diabetes
It results from a decrease in GFR during the second trimester
optionRationales: Glycosuria can be normal in pregnancy, so it does not confirm gestational diabetes on its own.
Glycosuria may be normal, but it may also indicate gestational diabetes, so it cannot simply be dismissed.
Correct. The higher GFR delivers more glucose than the tubules can reabsorb, which can cause glycosuria. Because it may also signal gestational diabetes, it needs follow-up.
The GFR rises by as much as 50% starting in the second trimester. It does not fall.
questions.rationale: Beginning in the second trimester, the GFR rises by up to 50%. Tubular reabsorption increases to compensate, but the kidneys may not be able to reabsorb all the filtered glucose, so glucose appears in the urine. That can be normal, or it can be a sign of gestational diabetes. The correct interpretation holds both possibilities and calls for follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy glycosuria: the higher GFR spills glucose. It may be normal or may be gestational diabetes, so follow up.
questions.hintContent: Connect the rise in GFR during pregnancy to the kidneys' ability to reabsorb glucose.
questions.hintStrategy: Be wary of options that say 'always' or 'confirms.' Look for the interpretation that explains the cause and still keeps the client safe.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Eight hours after a vaginal birth, a client has voided three times, 75 to 100 mL each time, and reports feeling as if her bladder is still full. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to increase her oral fluid intake
Teach the client Kegel exercises to strengthen her pelvic floor muscles
Document the voids as expected early postpartum diuresis
Perform a bladder scan after her next void to measure residual urine
optionRationales: More fluid will not help a bladder that is not emptying and can increase distention.
Kegel exercises help long-term pelvic floor strength but do not address possible retention now.
Early postpartum output increases, which would mean larger voids. Small, frequent voids with fullness are not expected.
Correct. Small, frequent voids with a sense of fullness suggest incomplete emptying. Postpartum clients are at risk for overdistention and residual urine, and a bladder scan shows how much remains.
questions.rationale: Postpartum clients are at risk for bladder overdistention, incomplete emptying, and residual urine, and urine output increases early after birth. Repeated small voids with persistent fullness suggest the bladder is not emptying, possibly with overflow. Measuring the residual confirms the problem before choosing an intervention. Fluids and Kegels do not address the immediate concern.
questions.takeaway: Postpartum: small frequent voids plus fullness suggest incomplete emptying, so check the residual.
questions.hintContent: Combine postpartum urinary risks with what small, frequent voids and a sense of fullness suggest.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you intervene. Choose the action that confirms whether the bladder is emptying.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The nurse is admitting an 82-year-old client. Which urinary findings are consistent with expected age-related changes? Select all that apply.
options: Wakes twice a night to void
Urine is pale and dilute
Small amount of urine remains in the bladder after voiding
New-onset urinary incontinence
Sudden, painful inability to void with a firm, distended bladder
Voids smaller amounts more often because the bladder holds less
optionRationales: Correct. Older kidneys excrete more fluid at night, so increased urine may interrupt sleep.
Correct. Reduced blood flow and a decreased ability to concentrate urine make it more dilute.
Correct. A more fibrous bladder leads to an increase in residual urine.
Urinary incontinence is never considered normal and often signals another medical problem.
Sudden, painful inability to void is acute retention, a medical emergency and not a normal change.
Correct. A more fibrous bladder has decreased capacity.
questions.rationale: Aging reduces blood flow to the kidneys, so urine becomes more dilute, and more fluid is excreted at night. The bladder becomes more fibrous, with decreased capacity and more residual urine. Incontinence and painful acute retention are never normal, even in older adults. They need follow-up because they often signal another medical problem.
questions.takeaway: Normal with aging: nocturia, dilute urine, smaller capacity, more residual. Never normal: incontinence or acute retention.
questions.hintContent: Recall the age-related urinary changes and the screening rule that incontinence and retention are never normal.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate gradual, expected changes from new or acute problems that need investigation.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: An 84-year-old client taking hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) for hypertension is newly confused. The client has dry mucous membranes, has been voiding large amounts of pale urine at night, and reports drinking little "so I don't have to get up." Urine specific gravity is 1.032. Which problem should the nurse address first?
options: Fluid volume deficit related to diuretic use and aging kidneys
Expected cognitive changes related to aging
Fluid overload from decreased kidney blood flow
Functional incontinence related to limited mobility and nighttime urgency
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults have a decreased ability to concentrate urine and excrete more fluid at night, which raises dehydration risk. A diuretic, low intake, dry mucous membranes, and a high specific gravity all point to fluid volume deficit.
New confusion is not an expected part of aging and needs a cause.
The cues (dry mucous membranes, high specific gravity, low intake) point to too little fluid, not too much.
No data in the stem suggest incontinence, and it would not explain the confusion or the lab result.
questions.rationale: Older adults are at increased risk of dehydration because they have a decreased ability to concentrate urine and excrete more at night. Diuretic use complicates these changes in concentration and electrolyte regulation. This client also limits fluids to avoid nocturia. Dry mucous membranes and a specific gravity above 1.030 confirm dehydration, which can cause confusion in an older adult.
questions.takeaway: Older adult plus diuretic plus limited fluids leads to dehydration. A specific gravity above 1.030 supports it.
questions.hintContent: Connect age-related changes in urine concentration, diuretic effects, fluid intake, and specific gravity.
questions.hintStrategy: Cluster the cues. Choose the problem that explains the most findings, including the new confusion.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Urinary Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The nurse teaches the parent of a 2½-year-old girl about toilet training. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I'll remind her to flush and wash her hands every time."
"We'll wait until she stays dry all night before working on daytime training."
"Most children gain control somewhere between 2 and 5 years, so I won't rush her."
"I'll teach her to wipe from front to back."
optionRationales: Toddlers need reminders about flushing and handwashing, so this is correct.
Correct. This statement needs correcting. Daytime control normally comes before nighttime control, so waiting for dry nights reverses the usual order.
Most children develop urinary control between 2 and 5 years of age, so this is correct.
Toddlers need instruction in wiping. Front to back is correct for girls.
questions.rationale: Most children develop urinary control between 2 and 5 years of age, and daytime control normally comes before nighttime control. Toddlers and preschoolers need reminders about flushing and handwashing and instruction in wiping. A plan that waits for nighttime dryness first misunderstands the usual sequence.
questions.takeaway: Toilet training: day before night, 2 to 5 years, and teach flushing, handwashing, and wiping.
questions.hintContent: Recall the toddler and preschool urinary milestones and teaching needs.
questions.hintStrategy: 'Needs further teaching' means looking for the incorrect statement. Check each against the normal developmental sequence.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four postoperative clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: Day 1 after bowel surgery: hypoactive bowel sounds, mild distention, and has not passed flatus yet
Day 2 after cesarean birth: reports crampy gas pains and is passing flatus
Day 2 after hip surgery: had a soft, formed, brown stool this morning
Day 3 after abdominal surgery: absent bowel sounds, vomiting, and a new rigid, tender abdomen
optionRationales: Slow bowel activity on the first day after bowel surgery is expected while peristalsis recovers from anesthesia and handling of the bowel.
Flatulence after cesarean birth is common, and passing gas shows the bowel is working.
A soft, formed, brown stool is normal.
Correct. Absent bowel sounds and vomiting on day 3 suggest a paralytic ileus, and a new rigid, tender abdomen raises concern for necrosis or perforation, which can follow an obstruction.
questions.rationale: Anesthesia and abdominal surgery slow bowel elimination, so some sluggishness early after surgery is expected. A paralytic ileus, in which intestinal muscles stop moving after surgery or drugs, carries a risk of bowel necrosis and perforation. Absent bowel sounds, vomiting, and a new rigid abdomen on day 3 suggest that complication. Gas pains after a cesarean and a normal stool are expected.
questions.takeaway: Paralytic ileus can lead to necrosis or perforation. A new rigid, tender abdomen needs assessment first.
questions.hintContent: Combine what is expected after anesthesia and surgery with the warning signs of a paralytic ileus and its complications.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out the expected findings, then choose the client whose findings are worsening and suggest a life-threatening complication.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.stem: A client has had frequent liquid stools for 2 days. Which findings should the nurse expect to monitor for in this client? Select all that apply.
options: More frequent bowel sounds
Redness and breakdown of the perianal skin
Dry mucous membranes and decreased urine output
Hard, dry stools
An urge to defecate that is easy to delay
Decreased bowel sounds
optionRationales: Correct. Diarrhea comes with cramps and more frequent bowel sounds because peristalsis is increased.
Correct. Frequent liquid stool irritates the skin and creates a risk for skin breakdown.
Correct. Diarrhea causes fluid and electrolyte losses, which show up as signs of dehydration.
Hard, dry stools describe constipation.
With diarrhea, the urge is difficult or impossible to control.
Increased motility produces more frequent bowel sounds, not fewer.
questions.rationale: Diarrhea is the passage of liquid feces with increased frequency. Faster peristalsis causes cramps, more frequent bowel sounds, and an urge that is hard to control. The main risks are fluid and electrolyte losses and perianal skin breakdown, so the nurse monitors hydration and skin.
questions.takeaway: Diarrhea: more frequent bowel sounds, a hard-to-control urge, fluid and electrolyte loss, and skin breakdown.
questions.hintContent: Link increased intestinal motility to the expected findings and complications of diarrhea.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each option fits fast motility and liquid stool, or slow motility and hard stool.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is documenting the stool characteristics of several adult clients. Which findings are expected in normal feces? Select all that apply.
options: Brown color
Soft but formed consistency
Small amounts of seeds or undigested meat fiber
Hard, dry pellets
Streaks of bright red blood
Watery, with no form
optionRationales: Correct. Normal feces are brown.
Correct. Normal feces are soft but formed.
Correct. Seeds, meat fiber, and fat may be present in small amounts in normal stool.
Hard, dry stools suggest constipation.
Blood is an abnormal constituent that needs follow-up.
Watery, unformed stool describes diarrhea.
questions.rationale: Normal feces are about 75% water and 25% solid material (bile, intestinal secretions, shed cells, bacteria, and minerals). They are brown and soft but formed, and they depend on normal fluid intake. Small amounts of seeds, meat fiber, or fat can be normal. Hard pellets, watery stool, and blood are not.
questions.takeaway: Normal stool: brown, soft, formed, about 75% water. Small amounts of seeds or fiber are OK. Blood is not.
questions.hintContent: Recall the composition and characteristics of normal feces.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option on its own: does it match the slides' description of normal stool?

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing causes of bowel obstruction. Which conditions cause a mechanical obstruction? Select all that apply.
options: Adhesions from a previous abdominal surgery
A hernia that traps a loop of intestine
Intussusception in an 18-month-old
Slowed intestinal muscle activity after general anesthesia
Paralytic ileus related to opioid medications
optionRationales: Correct. Adhesions physically block or kink the bowel, which makes them a mechanical cause.
Correct. A hernia is a physical blockage and a mechanical cause.
Correct. Intussusception, in which the bowel telescopes into itself, is mechanical and is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3.
When the intestinal muscles fail to propel contents after surgery, the obstruction is functional, not mechanical.
Paralytic ileus from drugs is a functional obstruction. Nothing is physically blocking the bowel. Peristalsis has stopped.
questions.rationale: A mechanical obstruction is a physical blockage, from adhesions, hernias, intussusception, volvulus, or tumors. A functional obstruction is a failure of peristalsis to push contents forward, as in paralytic ileus, where the intestinal muscles stop moving after surgery or drugs. Both risk bowel necrosis and perforation, but the cause is different.
questions.takeaway: Mechanical = something blocks the bowel. Functional = the bowel stops moving (paralytic ileus).
questions.hintContent: Distinguish a physical blockage from a loss of peristalsis.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: is something in the way, or has the bowel stopped pushing?

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.stem: A client admitted with diverticulitis has been receiving treatment for 2 days. Which new finding requires immediate follow-up?
options: Report from the last colonoscopy of several small outpouchings in the colon
Increased flatus after eating beans at lunch
Sudden severe abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen
One soft, formed bowel movement this morning
optionRationales: Outpouchings (diverticula) are already known in this client. They are the underlying condition, not a new complication.
Beans are a known cause of flatulence and this is not a danger sign.
Correct. Diverticulitis can cause perforation. Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen suggests the bowel has perforated, which is an emergency.
A soft, formed stool shows the bowel is functioning.
questions.rationale: Diverticular disease is outpouching of the colon where the lining herniates through the bowel wall. When the diverticula become inflamed (diverticulitis), the complications are obstruction, perforation, and bleeding. A sudden change to severe pain and a rigid abdomen signals perforation and needs immediate action. The other findings are known or expected.
questions.takeaway: Diverticulitis can lead to obstruction, perforation, or bleeding. A sudden rigid abdomen means possible perforation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the complications of diverticulitis and the cues that signal each.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a new, sudden change that matches a serious complication rather than a known or expected finding.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client asks what causes excessive intestinal gas. Which factors should the nurse include in the explanation? Select all that apply.
options: Chewing gum and drinking through a straw
Recent abdominal surgery
Eating foods such as beans and cabbage
Walking after meals
Drinking plenty of water during the day
optionRationales: Correct. Both lead to swallowed air, a cause of flatulence.
Correct. Abdominal surgery is a cause of flatulence because it slows bowel activity.
Correct. Certain foods are a cause of flatulence through bacterial action in the bowel.
Activity helps move gas through the bowel. It does not cause flatulence.
Adequate fluid supports normal bowel elimination and is not a cause of gas.
questions.rationale: Flatulence is excessive gas in the intestines or colon. Causes include bacterial action on chyme, swallowed air, gas diffusing from the bloodstream, certain foods, and abdominal surgery. Walking and adequate fluids support bowel function rather than causing gas.
questions.takeaway: Gas causes: bacteria acting on chyme, swallowed air, blood diffusion, foods, abdominal surgery.
questions.hintContent: Recall the listed causes of flatulence.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each option adds gas to the bowel or helps move it along.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: Four clients report concerns about their bowel habits. Which client's pattern meets the definition of constipation?
options: Has a soft, formed stool every other day and does not need to strain
Has passed two hard, dry stools in the past week with difficulty
Has a daily bowel movement and passes gas often after meals
Has two soft stools daily after starting to eat more fruit
optionRationales: A soft stool every other day is three or more a week and easy to pass, so it is not constipation, even if the client expects a daily movement.
Correct. Fewer than three bowel movements a week, with hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass, is constipation.
Daily bowel movements with flatus do not meet the definition of constipation.
Two soft stools a day within a normal range does not fit constipation.
questions.rationale: Constipation is fewer than three bowel movements per week, or difficulty passing stools that may be hard and dry. A stool every other day is within the normal range. A client who believes a daily stool is required has a perceived problem, not true constipation. Bowel frequency varies, so the definition looks at both frequency and how easily the stool passes.
questions.takeaway: Constipation: fewer than 3 BMs a week, or hard, dry stools that are hard to pass.
questions.hintContent: Recall the definition of constipation, including both frequency and stool character.
questions.hintStrategy: Count the stools per week for each client and check how easily they pass.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination: Physiology & Alterations
questions.stem: A 58-year-old client reports several recent episodes of being unable to control stool. Which understanding about fecal incontinence should guide the nurse's plan of care?
options: It is usually a symptom of another disorder whose cause must be identified
It is a normal part of aging that most clients learn to manage on their own
It is caused mainly by eating too much fiber in the diet
It is best managed by giving an antidiarrheal medication on a routine schedule
optionRationales: Correct. Fecal incontinence is usually a sign of another disorder, such as a neurologic disorder, depression, injury, inflammation, a mass, hemorrhoids, or an anal deformity. Finding the cause guides treatment.
Incontinence is not a normal change of aging, and this client is 58.
Fiber is part of prevention. It is not a cause of incontinence.
Routine antidiarrheals treat a symptom without identifying the cause, and they may be harmful depending on that cause.
questions.rationale: Bowel (fecal) incontinence is the inability to voluntarily control the passage of feces and gas through the anal sphincter. It is usually a manifestation of another disorder, such as a neurologic disorder, depression, trauma, inflammation, a mass, hemorrhoids, or anal deformity. The nurse's assessment therefore looks for the underlying cause rather than treating incontinence as normal or masking it with medication.
questions.takeaway: Fecal incontinence is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Look for the underlying cause.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the slides describe fecal incontinence and its possible causes.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the statement that leads to the most complete assessment rather than one that dismisses or masks the problem.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.stem: The nurse observes a nursing student performing an abdominal assessment on a client with constipation. Which action by the student requires correction?
options: Palpating all four quadrants and then auscultating bowel sounds
Inspecting the abdomen for distention and contour before touching it
Percussing the abdomen after auscultating it
Asking the client to describe the color and consistency of recent stools
optionRationales: Correct. This order is wrong. Auscultation must come before palpation, because palpating can change peristalsis and alter the bowel sounds heard afterward.
Inspection comes first, so this is correct.
Percussion after auscultation follows the correct sequence.
Asking about stool characteristics is part of the bowel history.
questions.rationale: The abdominal exam for bowel elimination uses inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation, in that order. Auscultation comes before palpation because pressing on the abdomen can stimulate or alter peristalsis and give a false picture of bowel sounds.
questions.takeaway: Abdomen: inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate. Listen before you touch.
questions.hintContent: Recall the order of the abdominal exam and why it differs from other body systems.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each action against the correct sequence and its reason.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.stem: The nurse assesses a client 2 days after creation of an ileostomy. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
options: Stoma that is moist and pink to red
Liquid to mushy output in the pouch
Firm, formed stool in the pouch
Stoma that is dusky purple to black
Peristomal skin that is red and weeping under the wafer
optionRationales: Correct. A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red, which shows good blood supply.
Correct. An ileostomy diverts stool from the small intestine before the colon absorbs water, so output is liquid to mushy.
Formed stool comes from a stoma farther along the colon, where water has been absorbed, not from an ileostomy.
A dusky or black stoma suggests poor blood supply and must be reported.
Red, weeping skin around the stoma is breakdown, often from contact with output, and needs ostomy care.
questions.rationale: Assessing an ostomy (ileostomy or colostomy) is part of the bowel assessment. Because the colon absorbs water, output becomes more formed the farther along the bowel the stoma is placed. An ileostomy, from the small intestine, produces liquid to mushy output and carries more risk of fluid loss. A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red. A dark stoma or broken-down skin around it is not expected.
questions.takeaway: Ileostomy: liquid output and a moist pink-red stoma. A dark stoma or weeping skin is not expected.
questions.hintContent: Connect where the stoma is in the bowel to how formed the output will be, and recall what a healthy stoma looks like.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each finding: does it fit a small-intestine stoma with good blood flow and intact skin?

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client is recovering after a colonoscopy during which tissue samples were taken. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
options: Mild cramping while passing flatus
Severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen and fever
A request for something to eat
Drowsiness that persists 30 minutes after the sedated procedure
optionRationales: Mild cramping and flatus are common as air used during the procedure is passed.
Correct. Severe pain with a rigid abdomen and fever after a colonoscopy with biopsy suggests perforation of the bowel wall, which is an emergency.
Wanting to eat is not a sign of a complication.
Drowsiness soon after the procedure is expected while sedation wears off.
questions.rationale: Colonoscopy lets the provider view the colon and take tissue samples. Afterward, mild cramping, flatus, and drowsiness from sedation are expected. A rigid, distended abdomen with severe pain and fever suggests the bowel was perforated, the same danger seen with other bowel alterations, and must be reported immediately.
questions.takeaway: After colonoscopy: cramping and gas are expected. A rigid, painful abdomen with fever suggests perforation, so report it.
questions.hintContent: Recall what colonoscopy involves and which findings signal bowel perforation.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate expected recovery findings and choose the one that matches a life-threatening complication.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with suspected bleeding in the esophagus or stomach is scheduled for a diagnostic test. Which test allows the provider to look directly at the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum?
options: Colonoscopy with tissue biopsy
Colorectal transit study
EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy)
Digital rectal examination (DRE)
optionRationales: A colonoscopy examines the colon, the lower part of the GI tract.
A colorectal transit study measures how quickly material moves through the colon.
Correct. EGD uses a scope passed through the mouth to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum.
A digital rectal exam assesses only the rectum and anus.
questions.rationale: The diagnostic tests for bowel elimination each view a different area. An EGD looks at the upper GI tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum). A colonoscopy views the colon and allows tissue samples. A colorectal transit study measures movement through the colon. A digital rectal exam assesses the rectum.
questions.takeaway: EGD = upper GI (esophagus, stomach, duodenum). Colonoscopy = colon.
questions.hintContent: Match each bowel diagnostic test to the part of the GI tract it examines.
questions.hintStrategy: Break the test names into their parts. The name often tells you what it examines.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.stem: During a bowel history, a client reports hard stools that are difficult to pass. Which client statements are cues that may be contributing to constipation? Select all that apply.
options: "I take an iron pill every morning."
"I've taken a laxative every night for years."
"I usually ignore the urge at work because the bathroom is far away."
"I drink about eight glasses of water a day."
"I walk my dog 2 miles every day."
"I eat oatmeal and fresh fruit every morning."
optionRationales: Correct. Iron is a medication known to contribute to constipation.
Correct. Ongoing laxative use inhibits the natural bowel reflexes and can cause constipation rather than relieve it.
Correct. Defecation habits matter, and ignoring or delaying the urge lets more water be absorbed from the stool, making it harder.
Adequate fluid is protective.
Regular activity supports bowel motility.
Fiber from whole grains and fruit is protective.
questions.rationale: The bowel history covers the defecation pattern, use of elimination aids, diet, fluid, exercise, medications, and stress. Iron, chronic laxative use, and ignoring the urge each contribute to constipation. Fluid, activity, and fiber are protective, so they are not contributing cues.
questions.takeaway: Constipation cues: medications (such as iron), chronic laxatives, and ignoring the urge. Fluid, fiber, and exercise protect.
questions.hintContent: Recall the components of a bowel history and which habits help or hurt bowel elimination.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each statement into 'risk' or 'protective' for constipation.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Assessment, Ostomies & Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 80-year-old client taking opioids has not had a bowel movement in 6 days and is now passing small amounts of liquid, foul-smelling stool. The client has a PRN prescription for an antidiarrheal. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the antidiarrheal medication as prescribed
Apply a barrier cream to protect the perianal skin
Increase the client's dietary fiber starting at the next meal
Check for a hard mass of stool in the rectum per protocol
optionRationales: Giving an antidiarrheal would slow the bowel further if the liquid stool is seeping around an impaction.
Protecting the skin is appropriate but does not address the likely cause.
Fiber helps prevent constipation but will not resolve an existing impaction and is not the first step.

Correct. Liquid stool after days without a bowel movement, in a client taking opioids, suggests stool seeping around an impaction. Assessing the rectum (digital rectal exam) confirms the problem before any treatment.
questions.rationale: The history (opioids, older age, 6 days without a bowel movement) points to constipation. Liquid, foul-smelling stool in that setting is a classic sign of fecal impaction, with liquid seeping around the hard mass. It is not true diarrhea. Assessment, including a digital rectal exam, comes first. Treating it as diarrhea with an antidiarrheal would make the impaction worse.
questions.takeaway: Liquid stool after days without a BM may be seepage around an impaction. Assess before giving an antidiarrheal.
questions.hintContent: Connect the risk factors for constipation with what liquid stool means in a client who has not had a bowel movement in days.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask what is really causing the liquid stool before choosing a treatment. Assessment comes before intervention.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a community group about preventing bladder and bowel elimination problems. Which recommendations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Maintain a healthy weight
Bear down with the pelvic floor muscles to push urine out faster
Go to the bathroom promptly when the urge to void or defecate occurs
Take a mild laxative every night to stay regular
Stop smoking
Limit fluids so you won't need the bathroom as often
optionRationales: Correct. Maintaining a healthy weight is a preventive lifestyle habit.
Prevention includes avoiding the use of pelvic floor muscles to force urine flow.
Correct. Good toileting habits include avoiding delayed voiding and defecation.
Routine laxative use inhibits natural bowel reflexes and can cause constipation.
Correct. Not smoking is on the list of preventive habits.
Adequate fluid intake is recommended. Limiting fluids concentrates urine and hardens stool.
questions.rationale: Prevention focuses on healthy lifestyle habits: a healthy weight, regular exercise, good toileting habits (not delaying voiding or defecation and not straining to force urine), adequate fluid and fiber, treating constipation or diarrhea as it occurs, not smoking, and avoiding bladder and bowel irritants. Nightly laxatives and fluid limits are common misconceptions that make problems worse.
questions.takeaway: Prevention: healthy weight, exercise, respond to the urge, fluids and fiber, no smoking, avoid irritants.
questions.hintContent: Recall the prevention habits listed for elimination and the misconceptions that work against them.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether each recommendation supports the body's natural elimination or works against it.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.stem: A client is planning a trip to a developing country. After teaching about modifiable risk factors for altered bowel elimination, which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: "I'll take a laxative each day of the trip so my bowels stay regular."
"I'll drink less water while I'm traveling so I don't need bathrooms as often."
"Handwashing and eating properly cooked and stored food will lower my risk of diarrhea."
"Since traveling is a nonmodifiable risk factor, there's really nothing I can do to lower it."
optionRationales: Daily laxatives are not preventive and can interfere with normal bowel reflexes.
Limiting fluids raises the risk of dehydration, especially if diarrhea occurs.
Correct. Poor hygiene, poor cooking and storage of food, and travel to developing countries are modifiable risk factors. Handwashing and food safety directly reduce them.
Travel is listed as a modifiable risk factor, and hygiene and food safety lower the risk.
questions.rationale: Modifiable risk factors for altered bowel elimination include poor hygiene, poor diet, poor cooking and storing of food, and travel, especially to developing countries. These can lead to diarrhea and its fluid and electrolyte losses. Handwashing and safe food handling address them. Laxatives and fluid restriction add new risks.
questions.takeaway: Travel, hygiene, and food handling are modifiable bowel risks. Teach handwashing and food safety.
questions.hintContent: Recall the modifiable risk factors for altered bowel elimination and what each could cause.
questions.hintStrategy: Find the statement that targets a listed modifiable risk without creating a new one.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client who reports no bowel movement for 4 days now has abdominal distention, vomiting, and no flatus. The client asks for the PRN laxative that is prescribed. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Hold the laxative and notify the provider
Offer a high-fiber snack and extra fluids
Give a stool softener instead of the laxative
Give the laxative to relieve the constipation
optionRationales: Correct. Distention, vomiting, and no flatus suggest a bowel obstruction. Laxatives are not used when a blockage is possible, so the nurse holds the dose and reports the findings.
Adding food and fiber when vomiting and no flatus suggest a blockage can worsen distention.
Swapping in a different bowel medication still does not address a possible obstruction, and that decision belongs to the provider.
Laxatives must not be used when an obstruction is possible, because increasing bowel activity against a blockage can lead to perforation.
questions.rationale: Laxatives are a collaborative therapy for constipation, but they are not used when a blockage or obstruction is suspected. Distention, vomiting, and absent flatus point beyond simple constipation to an obstruction, which carries a risk of necrosis and perforation and may require surgery. Holding the medication and reporting the findings is the safe first step.
questions.takeaway: Suspected obstruction: no laxatives. Hold the dose and notify the provider.
questions.hintContent: Connect the signs of bowel obstruction with the contraindication for laxatives.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether the findings fit simple constipation or something more serious, then choose the option that prevents harm.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client who gave birth vaginally 1 day ago has not had a bowel movement and says, "I'm afraid to go because it will hurt." Which collaborative therapy should the nurse anticipate?
options: An antidiarrheal agent to reduce stool frequency
A stool softener, with added fluid and fiber
A daily enema until bowel movements are regular
Holding food until the client has a bowel movement
optionRationales: An antidiarrheal would slow the bowel further and is not indicated.
Correct. A stool softener makes stool easier to pass, which reduces the pain the client fears. Fluid and fiber support regular elimination.
Repeated enemas interfere with natural reflexes and are not a routine postpartum measure.
Withholding food is not appropriate and does not address the fear of pain.
questions.rationale: After birth the bowels are sluggish, and pain may lead the client to delay elimination, which allows stool to harden. Stool softeners are one of the collaborative bowel therapies. Combined with independent measures such as encouraging fluid and fiber, a softener lets the client pass stool with less pain.
questions.takeaway: Postpartum fear of a painful BM: stool softener plus fluids and fiber.
questions.hintContent: Connect postpartum bowel changes and fear of pain with the purpose of each bowel medication class.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the therapy that makes defecation easier without harming natural bowel function.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An older adult in long-term care has occasional fecal incontinence. Which independent nursing interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Offer toileting shortly after breakfast to take advantage of the gastrocolic reflex
Teach pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises
Provide perineal hygiene promptly after each episode
Give an enema every morning to empty the bowel
Limit fluids in the afternoon to reduce stool volume
optionRationales: Correct. Bowel training uses the gastrocolic reflex after meals, which is especially important for older adults.
Correct. Pelvic floor exercises strengthen the muscles that control the anal sphincter.
Correct. Personal hygiene prevents skin breakdown from contact with stool.
Routine enemas require an order, interfere with natural reflexes, and are not an independent intervention.
Limiting fluids hardens stool and promotes constipation and impaction.
questions.rationale: Independent bowel interventions include encouraging fluid and fiber, teaching about diet, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, personal hygiene, and ostomy care. Scheduling toileting after meals uses the gastrocolic reflex, which older adults benefit from responding to. Routine enemas and fluid limits interfere with normal bowel function.
questions.takeaway: Bowel training, Kegels, and hygiene are independent. Use the gastrocolic reflex after meals.
questions.hintContent: Recall the independent bowel interventions and the role of the gastrocolic reflex in older adults.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the options a nurse can start without an order that support natural bowel control.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Interventions, Prevention & Risk Factors
questions.stem: The nurse is planning screening for elimination problems in an older adult clinic. Which statements about screening are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: There is currently no standard screening procedure for elimination problems
Verbal screening for abnormal symptoms should be part of regular checkups
Clients often need more direct questioning about elimination than about other health problems
Urinary incontinence is a normal part of aging and does not need follow-up
Urinary retention is expected in adults over 65 years of age
optionRationales: Correct. No standard screening procedures currently exist, so the nurse relies on assessment.
Correct. Verbal screening during regular checkups is recommended, especially for older adults.
Correct. Clients may be embarrassed and not volunteer symptoms, so direct questions are needed.
Urinary incontinence is never considered normal and often indicates another medical problem.
Urinary retention is never considered normal at any age.
questions.rationale: Because there is no standard screening test, nurses screen verbally at regular checkups, especially for older adults, and ask direct questions, since clients often do not bring elimination problems up on their own. Incontinence and retention are never normal and often point to another medical problem.
questions.takeaway: No standard screening exists. Ask directly at checkups. Incontinence and retention are never normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall the screening guidance and the 'never normal' rule on the slides.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each statement as true or false on its own. Watch for statements that normalize problems with aging.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The parent of a 3-week-old exclusively breastfed infant is worried because the baby's stools are loose, mustard yellow, and seedy-looking. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Firm, tan stools are normal at this age, so let's check for infection."
"Loose stools mean diarrhea, so you should switch to formula."
"Seedy stools suggest the baby is not digesting milk and needs testing."
"Mustard-yellow, seedy, soft stools are typical for breastfed babies."
optionRationales: Stools become firmer only after solids start, and tan stool is typical of formula feeding.
Soft, liquid stools are normal for young infants and do not mean diarrhea.
The seedy appearance is normal in breastfed infants and does not suggest a digestive problem.
Correct. Breastfed infants normally have mustard-yellow, seedy stools that are soft and liquid until solid foods begin.
questions.rationale: Infant stool depends on feeding. Breastfed infants have mustard-yellow, seedy stools, while formula-fed infants' stools range from tan to yellow to green. Consistency is soft and liquid until solid foods are started, and odor is faint until then. Reassurance and accurate teaching are the right response.
questions.takeaway: Breastfed: mustard yellow and seedy. Formula-fed: tan to yellow to green. Firmer stool comes with solids.
questions.hintContent: Recall how stool color and consistency differ between breastfed and formula-fed infants.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether the finding is normal for this infant's age and feeding method before choosing a response.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The pediatric clinic nurse receives four phone messages. Which child should the nurse call back first?
options: A 2-year-old who is not yet toilet trained
A 1-month-old breastfed infant who has six soft, yellow, seedy stools every day and feeds well
A 3-year-old who has occasional daytime accidents during toilet training
A 15-month-old with vomiting, a swollen abdomen, no stool for 24 hours, and bouts of crying
optionRationales: Bowel training is usually successful by 36 to 48 months, so a 2-year-old not yet trained is within the normal range.
Frequent soft, yellow, seedy stools are normal for a breastfed infant.
Occasional accidents are expected while a toddler is still learning control.

Correct. Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children under 3. Vomiting, distention, no stool, and episodes of severe pain suggest an obstruction, which risks bowel necrosis and perforation.
questions.rationale: Toddlers gain some bowel control between 1½ and 2 years and are usually trained by 36 to 48 months, and breastfed infant stool is normally soft, yellow, and seedy. A toddler with vomiting, a swollen abdomen, no stool, and episodes of severe pain has signs of obstruction. Intussusception is the most common cause at this age, and obstruction can lead to necrosis and perforation.
questions.takeaway: Under age 3, vomiting, distention, no stool, and pain episodes suggest intussusception. Call back first.
questions.hintContent: Recall normal bowel milestones for infants and toddlers, and the most common cause of obstruction under age 3.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out the normal developmental findings, then choose the child with signs of obstruction.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a pregnant client about bowel changes during pregnancy and after birth. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: "Higher progesterone levels slow the movement of stool through your intestines."
"Hemorrhoids are most common during the first trimester."
"Gas pains are common after a cesarean birth."
"Bowel movements usually speed up in the first days after birth."
"If you delay a bowel movement because you're afraid of pain, constipation can get worse."
"Your growing uterus will relieve bloating as the pregnancy progresses."
optionRationales: Correct. Elevated progesterone delays gastric emptying and decreases peristalsis, which can cause bloating and constipation.
Hemorrhoids are associated with late pregnancy.
Correct. Flatulence is common after cesarean birth.
Bowels are sluggish after giving birth.
Correct. Pain may lead to delaying elimination, which allows stool to harden.
The enlarging uterus aggravates symptoms rather than relieving them.
questions.rationale: During pregnancy, elevated progesterone delays gastric emptying and slows peristalsis, causing bloating and constipation, and the enlarging uterus makes this worse. Hemorrhoids appear late in pregnancy. After birth, bowels are sluggish, fear of pain may cause the client to delay elimination, and flatulence is common after cesarean birth.
questions.takeaway: Pregnancy: progesterone slows the bowel and hemorrhoids come late. Postpartum: sluggish bowels, pain-related delay, gas after cesarean.
questions.hintContent: Recall how hormones and the enlarging uterus affect the bowel during pregnancy, and the bowel changes after birth.
questions.hintStrategy: Check the timing and direction of each change: early or late, faster or slower, better or worse.

questions.ref: Module 5 · Elimination · Bowel Elimination Across the Lifespan
questions.stem: The nurse teaches an older adult about preventing constipation. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client says, "For about 6 weeks my stools have been narrower than usual, and I go back and forth between constipation and loose stools." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "A change like this that lasts for weeks should be checked by your provider."
"Try an over-the-counter laxative for a few weeks and see whether it helps you."
"Increase your fiber and we'll recheck this at your visit in 6 months."
"Bowel changes like this are a normal part of getting older."
optionRationales: Correct. A change in bowel habits over weeks should be referred to the primary care provider so the cause can be found, which may include diagnostic tests such as a colonoscopy.
Laxatives can inhibit natural reflexes and may hide a problem that needs evaluation.

questions.rationale: Older adults commonly have constipation, but a change in bowel habits that persists over weeks, such as a change in stool shape or alternating constipation and diarrhea, should be referred to the primary care provider. Evaluation may include tests such as a colonoscopy. Reassurance, self-treatment with laxatives, or waiting can delay diagnosis.
questions.takeaway: A change in bowel habits lasting weeks in an older adult: refer to the provider.
